Stage 1 · Warm-up

Warm-up

Six statements. You only have to care about one of them.

Choose the one statement you have the strongest opinion about — for or against.

Choose one, then write two lines saying what you think and why. Choose one, then tell your teacher what you think and why. Choose one, then compare with your partner and see whether you are on the same side.

1  Nobody has any privacy any more.
2  Home-made presents are better than expensive ones.
3  Modern art is a waste of money.
4  Life used to be simpler, and better.
5  The media only report bad news.
6  One person cannot protect the environment.

One only. There is no right answer — and you will not have to defend it yet.

Write it down

Write your opinion on the statement you chose. Two lines, no more. Keep it — somebody is going to disagree with it later.

Talk about it
  • Which of the six do people argue about most where you live?
  • Is there one you would never discuss with a stranger?
Now speak — ask and answer these questions with a partner.
Answer these two out loud before you go on.

1  Do you say what you think, or keep it to yourself?

2  When did you last change your mind about something?

Then tell the class the one most surprising thing about your partner.

Stage 3 · Grammar

Disagreeing without falling out

In English you almost never disagree straight away. You give something first.

Read these four replies from the recording.
  • I’m sorry, but I don’t really agree.
  • Yeah, but I don’t think that’s true.
  • I take your point, but I’m not sure about that.
  • True, but there are other ways to look at it.
All four disagree. What do most of them do before they disagree?
What to say, and when
What you are doingWhat you say
Asking for an opinionWhat do you think? · Do you agree? · How do you feel about that?
Giving an opinionIn my opinion… · I’d say that… · I think… · If you ask me…
AgreeingI completely agree. · That’s a good point. · Exactly. · You’ve got a point.
Half-agreeing, then disagreeingI take your point, but… · True, but… · Yeah, but… · Maybe, but…
Disagreeing softlyI’m afraid I disagree. · I’m not sure about that. · I don’t really agree.
No strong viewI haven’t really thought about it. · I don’t have strong views on this.
The shapegive a little  →  but  →  your own view. The word but is the hinge.
what you give first your own view

THE MOVE. Accept a little, then turn: I take your point, but…

SOFTENERS. I’m afraid, I’m not sure, not really — all of these mean “no” without the word.

INTONATION. The voice falls on but and rises again after it. Play the slider and copy it.

Not “You are wrong”, not “No, that is not true”, not “I disagree” with nothing before it.

This is the last new language of the unit. Everything else today is recycled.

THE MOVE. English disagreement almost always comes in two parts. First you give the other person something — True…, Yeah…, I take your point…, That’s a good point… — and only then you turn with but. Skipping the first part is not a grammar mistake, but it sounds much harder than you mean it to.

SOFTENERS. I’m afraid I disagree is not an apology; I’m afraid simply signals that what follows is unwelcome. I’m not sure about that and I don’t really agree do the same job. All three mean “no”, politely, and native speakers hear them as clear disagreement.

DEGREES. There is a scale here. I completely agree → You’ve got a point → I take your point, but → I’m not sure about that → I’m afraid I disagree. Choose your place on it deliberately; that choice does more work than any single word.

INTONATION. Listen to the four recorded replies in the slider. The voice steps down on but and then lifts. If you say the words flat, the politeness disappears — the tune carries as much meaning as the phrase.

Three things to avoid in English: “You are wrong” · “No, that is not true” · a bare “I disagree” with nothing in front of it. All three are correct English and all three will cool a conversation faster than you expect.

Worth knowing: I don’t have strong views on this is a complete, acceptable answer. You are allowed not to have an opinion.

Listen for the fall on but, then say it the same way.

Listen to five more replies. Is each one agreeing, half-agreeing or disagreeing?
1“You know, I think this is probably true.”
2“I’m afraid I don’t really agree.”
3“In my opinion, young people find it very hard to be alone.”
4“Yeah, I think you’ve got a point.”
5“I take your point, we do spend more time in contact now, but we still have quiet moments.”
Full grammar reference — Giving and answering opinions

Form

GivingIn my opinion… · I’d say… · If you ask me… · Personally, I think…
AgreeingI completely agree. · You’ve got a point. · Exactly.
Half agreeingI see your point, but… · I take your point, however…
Disagreeing politelyI’m not so sure about that. · I’m afraid I disagree.
PresentingFirstly… In addition… To sum up… Thanks for listening.

When and why we use it

  • There is a scale from full agreement to full disagreement; choose your place on it deliberately.
  • The softeners I’m afraid, I’m not sure and not really all mean ‘no’ without the word no.
  • Give the opinion, then the reason. An opinion with no reason invites an argument.
  • In a presentation, signal the structure out loud so the listener always knows where you are.

Signal words

in my opinion · personally · however · on the other hand · to sum up

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • To my opinion… → In my opinion…The preposition is in.
  • I am agree. → I agree.Agree is a verb, not an adjective.
  • I am not agree with you. → I don’t agree with you.Ordinary verb negation.
  • You are wrong. → I’m not so sure about that.Softer, and it keeps the conversation open.

Don’t confuse it with

I don’t agree is direct but acceptable. You’re wrong ends the discussion.

Stage 6 · The model

A two-minute presentation

Read it as a speaker, not as a reader. You are going to copy its shape.

The strangest museum I have ever visited

Good afternoon, everyone, and thanks for coming. I’d like to tell you about the strangest museum I have ever visited. It is under the sea.

Firstly, where it is. The park lies in the Caribbean, about eight metres down. The only way to see it is to dive.

Secondly, what is in it. A sculptor put the first statues there in 2006. One work is a ring of twenty-six figures holding hands. It took six months to make and weighs about fifteen tonnes, so he could not lower it in one piece — he put each statue down separately and joined them underwater.

In addition, there is a reason for it beyond art. The statues are made of a material that helps coral to grow, so a man-made object slowly becomes part of the environment. Fish move in. The sand shifts, and the figures look different from one month to the next.

In my opinion, that is the most interesting thing about the place. Most museums try to stop their objects changing. This one was designed to be changed.

To sum up: an underwater park, a sculptor with an idea, and a reef that is growing because of it.

Thanks for listening. Any questions?

Notice what is not there. No greeting longer than one line. No apology for being nervous. No list of everything the speaker knows. Six short blocks, one idea each, and an opinion clearly marked as an opinion.

Note. Written for this course. The underwater sculpture park it describes is real; the presentation is not a transcript.

Stage 7 · Now you

Now you

Two minutes on your feet, then the questions.

Useful language

Presenting — Good afternoon, and thanks for coming. · I’d like to tell you about… · Firstly… · Secondly… · In addition… · To sum up… · Thanks for listening. Any questions?

Giving your view — In my opinion… · I’d say that… · If you ask me…

Answering a hard question — That’s a good point. · I take your point, but… · I’m not sure about that. · I’m afraid I disagree. · I don’t have strong views on that.

1 · Prepare a two-minute presentation about something you find genuinely interesting.

A place, an object, a person, a habit — anything, as long as you could describe it to a stranger. Use the model’s six blocks and its four signposts. Notes only; you will speak, not read.

  • Greeting and subject — one line
  • Firstly — where or when
  • Secondly — what it is, with one concrete detail
  • In addition — something people do not expect
  • In my opinion — your own view, clearly marked
  • To sum up — one sentence, then Any questions?
2 · Work in groups of three. One presents, two listen and then question.
Card A — speaker

Two minutes, timed. Use all four signposts. Mark your opinion with In my opinion so the room can hear which part is fact and which is you. Finish with Any questions? and then actually wait.

Card B — audience

Listen without interrupting. Then each of you must do one thing: ask a real question, and disagree politely with something the speaker said. Use I take your point, but… or I’m not sure about that. Do not just say “interesting”.

Rotate until everyone has presented once and questioned twice. The questioning is where today’s language actually gets used.

Feedback
2 · You present, your teacher is the audience. Then swap.
Card A — you are the speaker

Two minutes, timed. Use all four signposts. Mark your opinion with In my opinion. Finish with Any questions? and wait.

Card B — your teacher is the audience

Listens without interrupting, then asks two real questions and disagrees politely with one thing. Then you swap: your teacher presents and you must question and disagree.

The swap matters more than the presentation. Disagreeing politely under pressure is the skill this lesson exists for.

Feedback
2 · Write your presentation out in full, then deliver it in two minutes.

Then close the page and say it. Record yourself if you can. Time it — two minutes, no more.

3 · Now answer three hard questions about it, out loud.

Imagine somebody in the audience says: “I’m not convinced”, “Isn’t that a waste of money?” and “Everybody says that.” Answer each one using I take your point, but…, I’m not sure about that and That’s a good point, although…
